title: Tagore and Gitanjali
objective: After this level you can explain how Rabindranath Tagore's songs became the first Nobel-winning work by a writer from outside Europe.
summary: Tagore's Bengali songs, sung wherever Bengali is spoken, became Gitanjali (1912) in his own English prose. In 1913 he became the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature.

cards.headline: In 1913 the Nobel Prize in Literature left Europe for the first time.
cards.body: It went to Rabindranath Tagore, a Bengali poet, and above all for a slim book of religious songs he had put into English prose himself. How did songs from Bengal become a prize-winning book in the West?

cards.headline: Song offerings
cards.body: The English Gitanjali (1912) is subtitled Song Offerings. It gathers Tagore's own prose translations of religious poems from several of his Bengali collections, with an introduction by the Irish poet W. B. Yeats. Poem 35 begins: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high;". In English they read as prose poems. In Bengal they were songs.

cards.headline: Songs before they were a book
cards.body: Tagore composed more than 2,000 songs, popular among all classes of Bengali society, and the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh are his. Yeats's introduction reports a Bengali doctor telling him the songs "are sung from the west of India into Burma wherever Bengali is spoken," and says Tagore "writes music for his words." This was poetry people carried in their voices.

cards.headline: In his own English words
cards.body: The 1913 prize motivation praises verse "by which, with consummate skill, he has made his poetic thought, expressed in his own English words, a part of the literature of the West." Yeats admitted what English readers missed: the Bengali originals, he was told, were full of "untranslatable delicacies of colour." The prize-winning book was the poet translating himself.

questions.prompt: Who made the English prose translations in Gitanjali (1912)?

options.label: A Bengali doctor Yeats met
options.rationale: He talked to Yeats about Tagore's fame.

options.label: The Nobel Prize committee
options.rationale: They judged the book; they didn't translate it.

questions.explanation: The English Gitanjali is Tagore's own prose translations from his Bengali collections, introduced by Yeats.

questions.prompt: Yeats was told the Bengali originals held "untranslatable" delicacies. So what did the 1913 prize citation actually praise?

options.label: The Bengali songs as sung in Calcutta
options.rationale: The citation names his English words.

options.label: Yeats's own rewritten versions of the poems
options.rationale: Yeats introduced the book; Tagore translated it.

options.label: A novel Tagore wrote in English
options.rationale: Gitanjali is a book of songs.

options.label: Tagore's poetic thought in his own English words

questions.explanation: The citation praises verse made part of Western literature "expressed in his own English words": the West met Tagore through his self-translation.

questions.prompt: Tagore's songs lived in singers' voices before they won a prize as a book. How, according to Level 6, did Homer's epics take shape?

options.label: Among singers who composed and reshaped them aloud
In a single manuscript written by one author
options.rationale: They grew from a long oral tradition.

options.label: As prose translations made by the poet himself
On clay tablets copied in a king's library

questions.explanation: Homer's epics grew from a centuries-old tradition of singers who inherited and reshaped stories as they composed aloud. Tagore's songs, too, lived first in singing.
